description: Belief Genome Project Probe Bank V2. 12 probes per dimension organized into 6 framing pairs. Each probe has explicit pair_id, orientation (canonical/inverted), frame_type, and expected_loading metadata for phase recovery in analysis.

schema.text: The probe statement shown to participants
schema.primary_dim: The single dimension ID this probe loads onto
schema.pair_id: Identifier shared with this probes framing-pair partner (p<dim>_<N>)
schema.frame_type: standard | personal | societal | edge_case | rotated_concrete | rotated_abstract
schema.expected_loading: Numeric weight on the primary dimension (0.0-1.0)
schema.direction: +1 for canonical, -1 for inverted (used in scoring)
schema.pair_partner_id: ID of the other probe in this pair (for phase analysis)

probes.text: An external physical reality exists whether or not anyone is there to perceive it.
Reality is a construction of the mind — without observers, the concept loses meaning.
When I close my eyes, the room around me continues to exist exactly as before.
I cannot really know what exists outside my own perception.
Communities can disagree about meaning, but the physical world they share is the same world.
Different cultures do not just describe reality differently — they live in genuinely different realities.
The laws of physics would still apply on a planet where no conscious being ever evolved.
Physical laws are descriptions humans invented; they have no existence apart from our minds.
A tree falling in an empty forest still produces vibrations in the air.
Sound, color, and texture only come into being when a mind encounters them.
Truth about the world is something we discover, not something we manufacture.
All facts are agreements among observers; there are no truths waiting to be found.
Some statements are true for everyone, in every culture, in every era.
Truth always depends on the culture, era, and perspective from which it is viewed.
When I think something is true, I expect it to be true for others as well.
What feels true for me may not be true for someone else, and that is fine.
A society without shared truths cannot hold itself together.
A healthy society makes room for many incompatible truths to live side by side.
Mathematical truths like 2+2=4 are absolute and unchanging.
Even mathematical truths only hold within a chosen system of rules.
Honesty is good and cruelty is bad, no matter where in the world you stand.
What counts as honest or cruel changes from culture to culture in important ways.
Without absolute truth, the very idea of being wrong loses its meaning.
Calling any belief 'absolute' is a sign that someone has stopped thinking about it.
The scientific method is the most reliable way humans have ever found to understand the world.
Science is one valuable tool among many — not the highest form of knowledge.
When I want to know something important, I trust peer-reviewed research over other sources.
On the questions that matter most to me, science usually has little to say.
Public policy should be built on the best available scientific evidence.
When science conflicts with values or tradition, science should not always win.
Even when the conclusions are uncomfortable, science gives us the closest thing to truth we have.
Science has limits it cannot see past, especially regarding meaning, beauty, and morality.
Vaccines, antibiotics, and modern medicine show that the scientific approach works.
Science gets things wrong often enough that it shouldn't be treated as the final word.
Reason and evidence outrank all other paths to knowledge.
Wisdom traditions, art, and spiritual practice can teach us things no laboratory will.
Gut feelings carry real information that careful analysis often misses.
Intuition is just habit and bias dressed up; it should not be trusted on important questions.
When something feels off, I trust that signal even if I can't explain it.
I try not to act on hunches until I can articulate solid reasons for them.
Communities should leave room for the wisdom that comes from instinct, not just calculation.
When groups follow intuition over evidence, they tend to make worse decisions over time.
Some people consistently sense things others cannot, and that ability deserves respect.
Claims about special intuitive ability rarely hold up to careful testing.
An experienced doctor's hunch about a patient often catches what tests miss.
I would rather an experienced doctor double-check with tests than rely on instinct.
Some forms of knowing happen below the surface of conscious thought.
What looks like 'deep knowing' is usually a story we tell ourselves after the fact.
Two opposing positions can both contain real truth at the same time.
If two claims contradict each other, at least one of them must be wrong.
I am comfortable holding two ideas in tension without resolving them into one answer.
When I notice I believe two contradicting things, I work hard to figure out which is right.
Healthy public debate requires acknowledging that opposing sides may each be partly correct.
Pretending opposing views are 'both right' is how societies avoid hard truths.
Light behaving as both wave and particle suggests reality itself can hold contradictions.
Apparent paradoxes always dissolve once we have a more careful description.
A person can be deeply kind and deeply selfish at the same time, and both descriptions can be true.
Calling someone both kind and selfish is loose talk — at heart, one will turn out to be the real one.
The deepest truths are paradoxical and resist being pinned down.
If you cannot state a truth clearly without contradiction, you do not understand it yet.
What I have lived through tells me more than any study could.
Personal stories are vivid but unreliable — large datasets give a truer picture.
I trust my own experience more than research that contradicts it.
When research and my experience disagree, I take the research seriously and revisit my view.
Policy should weight the testimony of people who have lived through something at least as heavily as the data.
Personal anecdotes mislead policymakers; we need representative data to govern fairly.
If a treatment helped me when statistics said it shouldn't, I trust what I felt.
If a treatment helped me when statistics said it shouldn't, the placebo effect is the most likely explanation.
A grandmother who raised five children knows things about parenting that no developmental study captures.
Generations of folk wisdom about parenting have been quietly corrected by careful research.
Knowledge that has not been earned through living is shallow knowledge.
Any genuine knowledge has to survive challenges that personal experience alone cannot provide.
Sitting with not-knowing is more honest than reaching for a quick answer.
Being uncertain for too long is a sign you have not done your homework.
I am genuinely comfortable saying 'I don't know' on important questions.
Not having an answer makes me uneasy, and I work to resolve it.
Public leaders are wiser when they admit the limits of what they know.
Leaders who say 'I don't know' too often lose the trust they need to act.
On the deepest questions of life, holding open mystery is wiser than picking a position.
Refusing to take a position on the deepest questions is its own kind of avoidance.
A scientist who says 'we don't yet know' is doing better work than one who fills the gap with a guess.
A scientist who refuses to commit to a working theory is failing at the job.
Doubt, kept honestly, is closer to truth than easy certainty.
Permanent doubt is a way of avoiding responsibility for what you actually believe.
There are deep patterns running through events; very little is truly random.
The mind is built to find patterns, but most of what we 'see' is statistical noise.
When something striking happens to me, I assume it carries a meaning.
When something striking happens to me, I treat it as coincidence until shown otherwise.
History repeats in patterns clear enough that we can learn from them.
'History repeats itself' is a story we tell — most situations are genuinely new.
Two strangers meeting twice in unrelated cities means something — that is not just chance.
Improbable coincidences happen all the time — that is what 'improbable' allows.
Numbers like birth dates, repeating sequences, or anniversaries can carry real meaning.
Reading meaning into birth dates or repeating numbers is a habit of mind, not a feature of the world.
The universe is structured at every level; pure randomness is almost an illusion.
Real randomness is woven into nature — not every event has a cause we can name.
Practices that have lasted for centuries probably contain wisdom worth keeping.
A custom being old is not a reason to follow it.
I lean toward keeping older ways of doing things until I see clear reasons to change.
I am happy to drop old ways the moment something better is on offer.
A society that loses touch with its traditions will lose its bearings as well.
Many traditions need to die for societies to grow into something better.
Even traditions we cannot fully explain often turn out to serve a purpose.
Many traditions persist mainly because we are afraid to question them.
Family rituals at meals, holidays, and milestones carry real value beyond nostalgia.
Family rituals can be meaningful or empty depending on the people, not the age of the custom.
What our ancestors learned about living should be respected, not casually overridden.
Each generation has the right to redesign its own way of living.
On technical questions, the considered judgment of qualified experts should usually carry the day.
Expertise is too often used to dismiss honest questions from ordinary people.
When a doctor, engineer, or scientist tells me something within their field, I take it seriously.
I do my own research and trust my judgment over a credential I have not vetted.
Public policy goes better when expert advice is taken seriously.
Communities should not hand important decisions to experts who do not share their lives.
Even when their conclusions are unpopular, qualified experts deserve a presumption of credibility.
When experts close ranks against dissent, that is a warning sign, not proof they are right.
If a panel of climate scientists agrees on a finding, that agreement carries real weight.
Even broad scientific consensus has been wrong before, and I keep that in mind.
Specialized training really does give people insight that the rest of us lack.
Ordinary people grappling with their own lives often see what credentialed experts miss.
Some kind of God or higher power exists in or beyond the universe.
There is no God or higher power; the universe is what it is, on its own.
I personally sense the presence of something greater than myself.
I have never had a genuine sense that anything divine is present.
Communities are healthier when they acknowledge a higher power above human authority.
Communities work better when they ground their values in human reasoning, not divine authority.
The fact that the universe is finely tuned for life suggests a creating intelligence.
The fine-tuning of the universe is better explained by physics and probability than by design.
Standing under a starry sky, I feel something divine looking back.
Standing under a starry sky, I feel awe at nature without inferring any deity.
Without a divine source, terms like meaning and purpose lose their footing.
Meaning and purpose can stand on their own without needing a god to ground them.
Organized religion provides goods that secular institutions cannot easily replace.
Organized religion has caused more harm than good across history.
Belonging to a religious community has been or could be valuable in my own life.
Belonging to a religious institution would feel constraining rather than nourishing for me.
Houses of worship play a vital role in holding communities together.
Religious institutions slow social progress more often than they help.
Even when individual leaders fail, the underlying religious tradition still has worth.
Repeated abuses by religious institutions reveal a deep flaw in the institutions themselves.
Charitable hospitals, schools, and shelters founded by religious groups have lifted many lives.
The same charitable work could be done — and often is — without religious institutions involved.
Shared rituals and shared moral language are gifts that organized religion offers.
Personal spirituality without an institution is more honest than belonging to a tradition.
Some part of who we are continues after the body dies.
When the body dies, the person ends — there is nothing more.
I expect to experience something after I die.
I expect death to be the end of my experience entirely.
Belief in an afterlife helps people behave more decently in this life.
People who believe this life is all there is take it more seriously.
Reports from those who have nearly died point to something real beyond the body.
Near-death experiences are vivid brain events, not glimpses of another world.
Dying loved ones sometimes seem to greet people who have already passed — that is not just a hallucination.
Visions reported by dying patients are gentle hallucinations, not contact with another realm.
It is wiser to live as if there is something on the other side than to assume there is not.
Living well in this life does not require any belief about what comes after.
Each person has a soul — a real, non-physical core of who they are.
What we call the 'soul' is a useful word for the brain at work — nothing more.
I feel that the deepest part of me is something more than my body.
When I look honestly, I am my body and my brain — no extra layer needed.
Treating people as souls, not just bodies, gives them deeper dignity.
Human dignity rests well enough on biology and shared humanity, with no need for a soul.
Identity in a brain-damaged person seems to point to something the damage cannot reach.

Newborn babies arrive with a clear individuality, as if the person was already there.
Differences between newborns are explained well enough by genes and womb conditions.
There is something at the center of a person that physics cannot fully describe.
A complete physical description of a person would, in principle, capture everything they are.
Prayer or meditation has effects in the world that go beyond their effects on the person doing them.
Whatever good prayer and meditation do, it stays inside the practitioner.
When I pray or meditate, I trust that something beyond my own mind is responding.
When I pray or meditate, I see it as a useful internal practice, not a conversation with anyone.
Communities that pray or meditate together genuinely send something out into the world.
Group prayer and meditation help the people in the room and stop there.
Prayer studies sometimes show effects that resist a fully natural explanation.
Careful studies of intercessory prayer have come up empty — that should mean something.
When I pray for someone who is suffering, I believe my prayer can actually help them.
Praying for a suffering friend mainly soothes the one praying.
Contemplative practice opens a real channel between us and reality at large.
Contemplative practice quiets the mind; that is its real and only gift.
Some events in our lives are meant to happen the way they do.
Nothing is fated; what happens is the result of choices and circumstances.
Looking back, I can see how my major life events were meant to unfold as they did.
My life has been shaped by chance and effort; nothing was 'meant' to happen.
Cultures handle hardship better when they trust that some things are out of their hands.
Cultures that lean too hard on fate end up tolerating injustice.
The way two strangers can meet at exactly the right moment suggests fate is real.
What feels like fate is usually selective memory — we forget the times nothing meaningful happened.
Meeting the person you marry after a chance reschedule is the kind of moment fate arranges.
Meeting your future spouse at a chance moment is just one path among many that could have happened.
Without some sense of destiny, life feels like a series of unconnected events.
Meaning comes from the choices we make, not from a path drawn for us in advance.
What you put into the world tends to come back to you in some form.
The universe does not balance moral accounts — only people and institutions can do that.
When I am generous, I notice good things tend to find their way back to me.
I have seen kind people suffer and cruel people prosper too often to believe in karma.
Societies do better when people trust that bad behavior eventually catches up with someone.
Counting on cosmic justice keeps people from doing the work of building real justice.
Even when justice is slow, the moral arc of the universe really does bend.
The history of injustice unpunished tells us no cosmic balance is at work.
A driver who cuts off others on the road tends, sooner or later, to find trouble of their own.
Reckless drivers usually go on driving the same way without consequences finding them.
Some moral law runs through reality, not just through human courts.
Morality is a human achievement, not a feature of the cosmos.
Some phenomena science cannot detect — ghosts, ESP, energies — are nonetheless real.
Stories of the supernatural have always evaporated under careful investigation.
I have personally experienced something I cannot explain in natural terms.
Anything strange I have experienced has had an ordinary explanation once I looked.
Cultures that take the supernatural seriously are tuned to something the modern world has forgotten.
Belief in the supernatural fades with education for good reasons.
Some skilled people really do know things they could not have known by ordinary means.
Apparent psychic abilities have not held up in any tightly controlled test.
Houses that feel haunted often turn out to have a real history connected to that feeling.
A 'haunted' feeling in a house comes from drafts, mood, and expectation, not spirits.
Reality is wider and stranger than the natural sciences currently allow.
What we call 'supernatural' is just a placeholder for things we have not explained yet.
Sacred texts contain literal historical and cosmological truths, not just stories.
Sacred texts are best read as poetry and history of ideas, not as factual reports.
When my own scriptures and modern findings disagree, I trust the scriptures.
Where my scriptures and modern findings disagree, I revise my reading of the scripture.
Public life suffers when scripture is no longer treated as factual.
Public life is healthier when scripture is treated as moral teaching, not literal history.
Where ancient texts describe miracles, the texts mean exactly what they say.
Ancient miracle stories are how people once expressed deep meaning, not factual reports.
When sacred texts give a timeline for creation, that timeline is meant as actual history.
Creation narratives in sacred texts speak to meaning and origin, not to chronology.
Treating scripture as metaphor strips it of authority.
Treating scripture as metaphor opens it up to deeper meaning, not less.
Genuine miracles — events that suspend the usual laws of nature — have happened.
What we call miracles always turn out to have natural explanations once we look closely.
Something has happened in my life that I would call a miracle.
What good fortune I have had has been ordinary luck, not anything miraculous.
Cultures lose something when they stop expecting miracles to be possible.
Belief in miracles often gets in the way of practical solutions to real problems.
Documented healings have happened that medicine alone cannot explain.
So-called miraculous healings reflect spontaneous remission and the power of expectation.
When a sick child recovers against all odds, something more than medicine has been at work.
When a sick child recovers against the odds, the odds are exactly the point — long shots happen.
The natural laws we know are real, but they are not the whole story.
Natural laws are exceptionless; that is what makes them laws.
Consciousness is a basic feature of reality, not a side effect of brains.
Consciousness is what brains do when they are organized in a particular way.
I sense that my own awareness is something more than the activity of my neurons.
My awareness, on close examination, looks like the brain in motion — nothing extra.
A culture that recognizes consciousness as fundamental treats nature with greater respect.
Treating consciousness as a brain phenomenon helps society make clear ethical decisions.
Even simple matter may have a faint inner experience, in line with deep theories of consciousness.
Inner experience requires highly complex information processing — rocks have none.
When meditation reveals awareness without thoughts, it is touching something more basic than the brain.
Pure-awareness states in meditation are remarkable brain configurations, nothing more.
Reality is built out of experience as much as out of matter.
Reality is built out of physical processes; experience emerges from them.
There is a real life energy in living beings that science has not yet measured.
What people call 'life force' is a metaphor for biological processes science already understands.
I can sometimes feel another person's energy without any obvious cue.
What seems like 'sensing energy' is really sensing posture, micro-expressions, and tone.
Traditional medicine systems describe real subtle energies that Western medicine misses.
Traditional energy medicine has rich symbolism but no measurable physical basis.
Practitioners of energy work can produce real effects in patients beyond placebo.
Studies of energy healers find effects no larger than placebo allows.
Acupuncture and qi gong work because they engage real energy channels in the body.
Acupuncture and qi gong have benefits explainable by nerves, expectation, and ritual.
Living things are different from non-living things in a way that is not just chemistry.
The difference between living and non-living things is fully captured by chemistry and physics.
The position of celestial bodies at someone's birth meaningfully shapes their personality.
Astrology has no real connection between celestial positions and a person's character.

Generic astrological descriptions feel like they fit because they fit almost everyone.
Astrology helps people reflect on themselves and their relationships in useful ways.
Astrology gives people false confidence about themselves and others.

Knowing someone's sign tells me something genuinely useful about them.
Knowing someone's sign tells me about astrology, not about them.
We are quietly connected to the larger cosmos in ways modernity has forgotten.
Our connection to the cosmos is a poetic feeling, not a causal influence.
We have lived in other forms before and will live again after this life.
We are born once, live once, and that is the full arc.
I have felt that some part of me has been here before.
I have never had any sense of having lived a previous life.
Cultures that take reincarnation seriously give people a longer view of their lives.
Belief in reincarnation can be used to justify accepting suffering that should be challenged.

Reported past-life memories in children turn out to be confabulation, not real recall.

Inborn talents are explained well enough by genetics and early environment.
The soul has many lives in which to grow and learn.
We have one life, and that single life is what gives our choices their weight.

A meaningful life does not require any spiritual practice at all.
I notice that when I keep up a spiritual practice, my life works better.
I have lived well without any kind of spiritual practice.

Societies do equally well or better when spiritual practice is a personal, not collective, matter.
Even people who say they are not spiritual end up developing some practice that serves the same role.
Many people live deeply meaningful lives with no rituals you would call spiritual.
Daily prayer, meditation, or contemplation deserves time as much as exercise does.
Treating spiritual practice as a daily must turns it into another chore.
A life without inner practice loses depth, no matter how busy it is on the outside.
Depth comes from how we live and love, not from any specific practice.
Some actions are wrong everywhere, regardless of culture or circumstance.
What counts as right and wrong depends on the culture and moment one is in.
When I say something is wrong, I mean wrong for everyone, not just for me.
When I judge an action wrong, I know I am speaking from my values, not universal truth.
Societies need to share certain non-negotiable moral principles to function.
Plural societies do better when they treat morality as something to be negotiated, not handed down.
Torturing innocent people for fun is wrong everywhere, full stop.
Even acts that seem unspeakable to us were honored in some cultures — moral truth is not universal.
Slavery was always wrong, even when entire societies accepted it.
Calling past societies 'wrong' by today's standards misses how morality actually develops.
Without universal moral truth, the idea of moral progress collapses.

I would resist giving up my own freedoms even for clear collective benefit.
I am willing to accept limits on my freedom when the community needs me to.

Societies that elevate individual rights above all else lose the bonds that hold them together.
Even during emergencies, basic individual rights should not be suspended.
In a true emergency, individual rights have to give ground to the safety of the group.

When public health is at stake, asking individuals to comply with medical measures is reasonable.
The individual is the basic moral unit; groups derive their worth from the people in them.
Individuals are partly constituted by the communities that raise them; pure individualism is a fiction.
What matters morally is the intent behind an act, not just how it turns out.
What matters morally is the actual outcome, not what the person was trying to do.
If I tried to help and accidentally hurt someone, I am still in the moral right.
Good intentions do not let me off the hook for the harm I have caused.
Laws and institutions should weigh what people meant to do, not only what happened.
Public morality should focus on outcomes; intentions are too easy to claim.
A failed attempt at murder is morally as serious as a successful one.
A failed attempt is genuinely less bad than a completed harm — outcomes matter.
A driver who tried to swerve and still hit someone is less blameworthy than one who did not try.
Whether the driver tried to swerve is far less important than what happened to the person they hit.
Moral worth lives inside our reasons, not in the world's response to our actions.
Morality is ultimately about effects in the world, not about the inner life of the actor.
Long-standing moral codes deserve more trust than recent ethical innovations.
Each generation has the right and the responsibility to revise the moral codes it inherited.
When making a hard moral choice, I look first to the wisdom of older traditions.
When making a hard moral choice, I look first at the situation in front of me, not at tradition.
Public morality drifts when communities cut themselves off from inherited ethical traditions.
Communities grow morally by questioning inherited norms, not by clinging to them.
Even when traditional moral codes seem harsh, they usually have a reason worth understanding.
Many traditional moral codes simply protected the powerful at the expense of the rest.
Older norms about honesty, fidelity, and duty still steer us better than modern alternatives.
Updated norms about honesty, fidelity, and duty fit modern life better than the older ones.
Inherited moral wisdom is the closest thing we have to time-tested knowledge of how to live.
Inherited moral wisdom is, at best, a starting point — never the final word.
Strong punishment is the main reason people refrain from doing wrong.
Most people behave well because they internalize values, not because they fear punishment.
I am more likely to follow a rule when I know there are real consequences for breaking it.
I follow rules because I see the point of them, not because I am afraid of getting caught.
Communities are safer when wrongdoing is met with firm and predictable punishment.
Communities are safer when they invest in prevention and rehabilitation rather than punishment.
Without fear of consequences, far more people would harm others to get what they want.
In countries with mild punishments, people generally do not act worse than in those with harsh ones.
Tougher sentences for repeat offenders make neighborhoods safer over time.
Stacking longer sentences on repeat offenders does little to make neighborhoods safer.
Justice that does not bite is no justice at all.
True justice aims at restoring relationships, not at hurting wrongdoers.
It is morally wrong for some people to have enormous wealth while others lack basic needs.
Inequality of wealth is not by itself a moral problem; how the wealth is gained is what matters.
When I see extreme wealth alongside extreme poverty, I feel something is morally off.
Seeing someone wealthy near someone poor does not, by itself, strike me as unjust.
A society where the gap between rich and poor keeps widening is failing morally.
A society can be morally healthy with wide income gaps as long as opportunity remains broad.
Even great wealth honestly earned is hard to justify alongside avoidable suffering.
Wealth honestly earned is the wealth-holder's to keep; suffering elsewhere does not change that.
A billion-dollar fortune in a country with widespread hunger is a moral failure.
A billion-dollar fortune is not unjust on its own; what its holder does with it is the moral question.
Justice requires actively narrowing the gap between the most and least well-off.
Justice requires fair rules, not equal results.

An unborn human life has moral weight that limits the choice to end a pregnancy.
I respect a person's decision to end a pregnancy as their own to make.
I see ending a pregnancy as a serious moral act that should not be treated lightly.
Laws should leave the abortion decision to the pregnant person and their doctor.
Laws should reflect a society's stake in the life of the unborn.
In hard cases like rape, incest, or threat to the mother's life, ending a pregnancy is morally defensible.
Even in difficult cases, the moral weight of an unborn life remains, and exceptions should be narrow.
Bodily autonomy means a person cannot be required to carry a pregnancy against their will.
Bodily autonomy has limits when another developing life is at stake.
A society's respect for women is reflected in its respect for their reproductive choices.
A society's respect for human life is reflected in how it protects the most vulnerable, including the unborn.
Some crimes are so severe that the death penalty is a just response.
It is wrong for the state to deliberately end a person's life, even for a serious crime.
I could in good conscience support a death sentence for the worst crimes.
I could not in good conscience support the state taking a person's life.
Capital punishment can be a fitting expression of a society's most serious moral judgments.
Capital punishment lowers a society to the level of the violence it claims to condemn.
For mass murderers and terrorists, the death penalty is a defensible last response.
Even for the worst offenders, the risk of executing the innocent is a reason to do without it.
A killer who has taken many lives has forfeited the right to keep their own.
Even a killer who has taken many lives still holds a basic right to life.
Justice sometimes asks for the strongest possible response, including death.
A society best expresses justice by refusing to take life, no matter what the offense.

Even highly intelligent animals do not warrant protections at the level humans receive.

Modern farming, including large-scale operations, is a reasonable way to feed billions of people.

Human suffering matters in a category of its own, distinct from animal suffering.

Each generation will solve its own environmental problems with the technologies of its time.
